case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal statutes fixing a single nationwide ‘Election Day’ for choosing presidential electors and Members of Congress preempt Mississippi’s law allowing absentee ballots that were cast/mailed by Election Day to be received and counted up to five business days after Election Day.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. art. I, § 4, cl. 1 (Elections Clause); U.S. Const. art. II, § 1, cl. 4 (Presidential Electors Clause); federal ‘Election Day’ statutes setting the day for choosing Representatives (2 U.S.C. § 7), Senators (2 U.S.C. § 1), and presidential electors (currently codified at 3 U.S.C. § 1); and Miss. Code Ann. § 23-15-637(1)(a) (Mississippi’s absentee-ballot receipt deadline allowing receipt up to five business days after Election Day).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Mississippi (through its Secretary of State) argues that its receipt-deadline rule is a valid exercise of state authority over the ‘Times, Places and Manner’ of elections and does not conflict with the federal Election Day statutes because the election is still ‘held’ on Election Day when voters must cast/submit ballots by that day; allowing election officials to receive and count timely-cast absentee ballots after Election Day is an administrative tabulation/processing rule rather than an impermissible extension of Election Day itself. Mississippi also invokes structural and purposive arguments (including UOCAVA and the idea that Congress would not intend to impede voting) to support interpreting the federal Election Day statutes as not forbidding post-Election-Day receipt of timely-cast ballots, warning that the Fifth Circuit’s contrary view risks disenfranchising lawful voters (especially those who vote absentee, including covered voters) and upsetting widespread state practices.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The RNC and aligned respondents contend that Mississippi’s rule conflicts with—and is therefore preempted by—the federal Election Day statutes because permitting ballots to be received and counted after Election Day means the election is effectively still ongoing and not ‘consummated’ on the federally mandated day; the federal scheme requires that the decisive act of voting for federal offices be completed on the uniform national date, and a state cannot extend the time at which votes may be added to the count beyond that date. They further argue the Fifth Circuit properly applied Supreme Court and circuit precedent (especially Foster’s understanding of ‘the day’ Congress selected) and that Mississippi’s attempts to distinguish those cases fail; leaving the issue unresolved, they say, invites uncertainty and strategic behavior in close races where late-arriving ballots can change outcomes.
key_precedents: Republican National Committee v. Democratic National Committee, 589 U.S. 423 (2020) (per curiam)
Voting Integrity Project, Inc. v. Bomer, 199 F.3d 773 (5th Cir. 2000)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest point: the federal statutes speak only to the “day” for holding the election, and Congress legislated against a backdrop of post‑Tuesday receipt, verification, and tabulation. But Mississippi’s rule does not simply recognize an administrative tail; it makes legal countability depend on a post‑Day event—receipt—so outcome‑determinative ballots may still enter the electorate after Congress’s fixed day, implicating Foster’s focus on when the election is “consummated” as the combined actions of voters and officials. Smiley’s recognition of broad state authority over election mechanics does not answer a direct conflict with Congress’s time‑setting statutes, and I am not persuaded that historical practice “liquidates” those statutes into an implicit authorization for receipt windows. If Congress wishes to permit ballots cast by Election Day to be received afterward for federal offices, it can do so expressly.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is that Mississippi makes countability turn on a post–Election Day event (receipt), so the legally operative pool of ballots remains “open” after Tuesday in Foster’s “consummation” sense. But that reading effectively converts Congress’s uniform-“day” statutes into a federal receipt deadline Congress did not enact, and it invites federal courts to supply supervisory detail the Elections Clause assigns to Congress—not us. As Justice Alito and Justice Kagan emphasize, Mississippi fixes the voter’s decisive act (timely casting/mailing as evidenced by a postmark) by Election Day; what follows—receipt, verification, and tabulation—is the ordinary administrative tail that necessarily continues after polls close and has long been left to the States absent a clear congressional command. Given Purcell’s caution against late judicial reshaping of election rules and the absence of a clear federal directive on receipt deadlines, I would not extend Foster beyond its “too-early election” context to preempt this regime.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is that Mississippi makes countability turn on a post–Election Day event (receipt), and they invoke Foster’s “consummation” language to argue the legally operative electorate remains open after the federal day. But that theory effectively converts §§ 1 and 7 into a federal receipt-and-eligibility deadline Congress did not enact and, as Justice Kagan notes, would extend Foster well beyond its “too-early” context in a way that destabilizes longstanding, widespread absentee practices without a clear congressional command. Here, the legally decisive voter act is fixed by Election Day (timely casting/mailing with a postmark), and the ensuing receipt/verification is the ordinary administrative tail that States have historically managed; treating that tail as preempted would read spare federal text to “uproot” entrenched, facially neutral time-place-manner rules. On this record, the State’s interests in orderly administration and election integrity support a short, fixed receipt window that does not meaningfully extend the day of choosing federal officers.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is that Mississippi makes countability turn on a post–Election-Day event (receipt), leaving the “legally operative universe” open after Tuesday. But that argument effectively reads Foster’s “consummation” language to impose a federal receipt-and-counting deadline nowhere stated in 2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7 or 3 U.S.C. § 1, and it treats routine post-Day administrative mechanics as a prohibited extension of the federally fixed “day” without the clear congressional instruction we ordinarily require for Elections-Clause displacement. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, Foster addressed a different structural defect—States completing selection before the federal day—and I do not see a precedent-grounded basis to expand it into a novel presumption that any postmarked-by-Tuesday ballot must also be received by Tuesday. Where Mississippi fixes the voter’s decisive act by Election Day (timely cast/mailed and postmarked) and only allows a short, definite receipt window, I would not have this Court supply a new federal rule Congress has not enacted.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s best point is that Mississippi’s rule leaves the legally countable pool of ballots “open” after Election Day because receipt occurs later, and Foster speaks of an election as the “combined actions of voters and officials.” But Foster addressed the opposite uniformity problem—States trying to finish (and effectively decide) elections before the federally fixed day—and its “consummation” language should not be extended to create, by implication, a hard federal receipt deadline absent any such instruction in 2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7 or 3 U.S.C. § 1. Where the federal text is spare, the longstanding and widely known practice of counting timely-cast absentee ballots received shortly after Election Day supplies strong constitutional and statutory “gloss” that liquidates “Election Day” as fixing the voter’s act of choice, while recognizing an inevitable administrative tail. Justice Barrett’s concern about eligibility turning on later events is serious, but here eligibility is fixed by Election Day (postmark/mailed-by), and the later receipt condition is part of ordinary election administration that Congress has not clearly displaced.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh rightly press that Mississippi’s rule makes countability depend on a post‑Day event (receipt), so the “pool” of ballots can change after Tuesday. But the federal statutes Congress enacted—2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1—speak only to the “day” for holding the election, and they supply no clear textual hook for converting that command into a federal receipt deadline, especially against the backdrop of longstanding administrative practice of receiving and counting timely cast absentee ballots after Election Day. As Justice Kagan notes, Foster’s “consummation” language arose to stop States from effectively deciding elections before the federal day; extending it to forbid post‑Day receipt would import a voter/official completion rule the text does not express and would upset entrenched practice without a clearer congressional instruction. The better coherence is to treat the voter’s decisive act as fixed by Election Day (here, timely postmark/submit-by), with later receipt and canvass as ordinary ministerial steps that do not themselves change the federally fixed “day” of the election.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch make the best point that the federal statutes speak only to the “day” of the election and that Congress legislated against a backdrop of post‑Tuesday receipt, verification, and counting. But that argument elides the discrete structural question: Mississippi’s rule does not merely permit continued tabulation of timely cast votes; it makes legal countability turn on a post‑Election‑Day event (receipt), meaning outcome‑determinative ballots can enter the legally eligible pool after the federally fixed day. As the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, that feature implicates Foster’s “consummation” concept because the combined actions that determine the legally operative choice are not complete on the uniform federal day, risking a state-by-state patchwork in the timing of when federal elections are finally fixed. Absent a clearer congressional authorization for post‑day receipt windows, I would adhere to preemption and leave any adjustment to Congress.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch press the hardest textual point: §§ 1 and 7 speak only of the “day” for holding the election, and longstanding post‑Tuesday receipt/count practice supplies some interpretive gloss. But that gloss fits ministerial post‑day tabulation of votes already legally cast; Mississippi instead makes legal countability hinge on a post‑Day event (receipt), leaving the operative electorate open beyond the uniform federal day, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize. Foster’s “consummation” language, though arising in a too‑early context, is still the best account of Congress’s uniformity command because it targets state rules that shift when the legally operative choice is fixed, not merely when officials finish counting. Absent clearer evidence that the original public meaning of “the day” encompassed a multi‑day accrual of newly eligible votes, I would treat the federal timing statutes as preemptive and leave any receipt‑window authorization to Congress.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is that Mississippi’s receipt-by-five-business-days rule makes countability turn on a post–Election Day event, leaving the “legally operative universe” open after Tuesday in a way they say triggers Foster’s “consummation” language. But I remain unpersuaded that Foster should be extended from its distinct “too-early” context into a judge-made federal receipt deadline that Congress did not clearly enact in 2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7 or 3 U.S.C. § 1—especially given the longstanding, widely known practice of post-Day receipt, verification, and tabulation of timely cast absentee ballots that Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch highlight. Structurally, the uniform-day statutes can be read narrowly to fix the voter’s decisive act of choosing by the federal day (as Mississippi does via postmark/submit-by), while leaving the inevitable administrative tail to the States absent clearer congressional displacement. Treating the receipt condition as constitutionally or statutorily dispositive would risk unnecessary federal intrusion into state election administration and create non-textual national rules better left to Congress to prescribe explicitly if it wishes.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Elections Clause and Presidential Electors Clause give States broad authority to prescribe a “complete code” for federal elections—including rules for casting and counting ballots—but that authority operates subject to Congress’s express power to “make or alter” state regulations and to fix the day for choosing federal officers. Congress has exercised that power through 2 U.S.C. §§ 1, 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1, and our decision in Foster reads those statutes to require that the “combined actions of voters and officials” culminating in a final selection occur on the uniform national day. Mississippi’s rule permits additional valid votes to be received and added to the count after Election Day, so the electorate’s final selection is not complete on the federally mandated day, creating a conflict that the federal statutes preempt. Whatever the policy arguments for a receipt deadline, it is for Congress—not this Court—to revise the uniform-day command if it wishes to accommodate multi-day receipt windows.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under the Elections Clause and the Presidential Electors Clause, Mississippi’s legislature has primary authority to prescribe the manner of federal elections, and Congress’s Election Day statutes should not be read to displace that state-law choice absent a clear conflict. Mississippi’s rule does not extend the time when ballots may be cast by voters: it requires absentee ballots to be cast/mailed and postmarked by Election Day, and merely allows election officials to receive and count those timely-cast ballots within five business days. Because the decisive act of voting occurs on the federally designated day, this looks like a permissible administrative receipt-and-tabulation rule rather than an alteration of the election’s “day” itself. Reading the federal statutes to preempt such a rule would invite federal-court supervision of election administration that the Constitution assigns primarily to state legislatures (subject to Congress), and Foster does not compel treating post-Election-Day receipt of timely-cast ballots as an impermissible extension of Election Day.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes “simply regulate the time of the election” and require that the decisive act of voting occur on the uniform national day, but they do not clearly displace facially neutral state rules governing the mechanics of casting, receiving, and tabulating timely-cast ballots. Mississippi’s law requires voters to cast/mail their absentee ballots by Election Day and merely allows election officials to receive and count those timely-cast ballots for five business days thereafter—an administrative receipt-and-processing rule that does not select any officeholder before the federal day. Given the widespread, longstanding use of absentee voting regimes that necessarily involve post–Election Day processing, and absent a clear congressional command that all ballots must be received by Election Day, I would not read the federal statutes to uproot this traditional “time, place, and manner” regulation. The record-driven concern for election integrity and confidence is weighty, but a brief, fixed grace period for timely-mailed absentee ballots—rather than an open-ended extension—does not, on this record, establish a conflict sufficient to warrant preemption.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Our task is doctrine-bound: the federal Election Day statutes fix a uniform day for choosing federal officers, but preemption requires a clear conflict between federal timing mandates and the State’s regulation of election “manner” and administration. Read in light of Foster v. Love—which held States may not “consummate” the election before the federal day, while acknowledging that election mechanics naturally occur before and after that day—Mississippi’s rule does not move the decisive act of choosing beyond Election Day because voters must cast/mail absentee ballots by that date and the post-Day window governs only receipt, verification, and tabulation of timely-cast votes. Absent on-point precedent squarely equating “Election Day” with a federal prohibition on counting timely-cast ballots received shortly afterward, I would not adopt a novel presumption of preemption that displaces a State’s traditional administrative authority over how votes are collected and counted. Any contrary rule should come from Congress in unmistakable terms, not from extending Foster beyond its holding to invalidate widespread, long-accepted election-administration practices.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The constitutional text Congress implements here is spare: the Elections Clause and Presidential Electors Clause let Congress set the “Times” (and the “Time of chusing” electors), but they do not themselves specify that ballots must be received—and not merely cast or mailed—by that day. Mississippi’s rule keeps the decisive act of choosing on the federally fixed Tuesday because voters must submit their absentee ballots by Election Day; the later receipt and canvass of timely cast ballots is the kind of post‑Day administration that any system necessarily entails, and nothing in the federal Election Day statutes expressly forbids it. Longstanding national practice confirms that understanding: for much of our history States have counted timely cast ballots received after Election Day (especially for absentee and overseas voting), a “regular course of practice” that helps liquidate the meaning of barebones “Election Day” language toward fixing the deadline for voters’ choice rather than the deadline for officials’ processing. Foster is best read to bar States from consummating federal elections before Election Day (as Louisiana attempted), not to prohibit States from completing the ministerial tasks of receiving and counting ballots timely cast by Election Day; on that view, there is no conflict and thus no preemption.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes fix “the day” for choosing federal officers, but their text speaks to when the election is “held” or the choice is made—not to when election officials must finish receiving and canvassing ballots that voters timely cast (or mailed with a postmark) by that day. Reading those enacted words against the backdrop of longstanding nationwide administrative practice—where States commonly tabulate, canvass, and certify after Election Day, and often accept timely-cast absentee ballots arriving shortly thereafter—I would presume Congress legislated with that settled understanding in mind absent clearer textual direction. Nothing in §§1, 7, or 3 U.S.C. §1 supplies the clear indication needed to overcome that presumption by transforming a voting deadline into a hard receipt-and-tabulation deadline, and I see no warrant to add that extra-textual distinction here. Properly read, Mississippi’s rule still requires the voter’s decisive act of choosing to occur by Election Day and thus does not conflict with (and is not preempted by) the federal statutes.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The discrete question is whether Mississippi’s rule allows the legally operative act of “choosing” federal officers to remain open after Congress’s nationally fixed Election Day, thereby conflicting with the federal Election Day statutes enacted under the Elections Clause and Presidential Electors Clause. Those statutes implement a structural judgment for national uniformity; allowing some States to add counted votes for days after Election Day risks a multi-State patchwork regime in which the decisive electorate differs depending on local receipt deadlines, with predictable systemic consequences in close federal contests. Under Foster, the pertinent inquiry is when the election is “consummated”—the time when voter and official actions together produce the final selection—and Mississippi’s five-business-day window for receipt and counting of ballots extends that consummation beyond the federally prescribed day. Because Congress has exercised its superior authority to set the time for federal elections, Mississippi’s conflicting timing rule must yield under Elections-Clause preemption.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes fix a single national day for “choosing” Representatives, Senators, and presidential electors, and the best textual reading—confirmed by their historical purpose of ensuring a uniform, consummated federal choice—does not permit States to continue adding votes to the count after that day in a way that can change the outcome. Mississippi’s rule makes the set of ballots eligible to be counted depend on post–Election Day events (receipt within five business days), so the federal election is not fully “held” on the Tuesday Congress selected. Under the Elections Clause and Presidential Electors Clause, Congress’s time-setting enactments are paramount and preempt inconsistent state regulations, even if the State characterizes the extension as mere “administration.” Foster’s understanding that federal law requires the election to be completed on the federally prescribed day supplies the controlling framework, and Mississippi’s contrary interpretation would undermine the uniformity Congress mandated.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Constitution’s structure gives Congress authority to fix a single national “Time” for choosing Representatives, Senators, and presidential electors, but it leaves States substantial room to regulate the “manner” of administering elections—including the mechanics of absentee voting—so long as state rules do not undermine national uniformity in the sense of permitting votes to be cast after the federally set day. Mississippi’s law requires voters to cast/submit absentee ballots by Election Day and merely allows election officials to receive and count those timely-cast ballots for a short, defined period afterward; that looks like an administrative tabulation/receipt rule within the State’s retained election-administration authority rather than a state effort to move the decisive act of choosing federal officers off the uniform national date. Reading the federal Election Day statutes to preempt this kind of post-day receipt window would unnecessarily extend federal displacement into routine election administration, despite the absence of a clear congressional directive that “Election Day” regulates the deadline for officials’ receipt of timely-cast absentee ballots. On this narrower structural ground, Mississippi’s rule does not create the sort of nonuniform, state-by-state extension of when voters may choose federal officers that Congress sought to foreclose.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal “Election Day” statutes preempt Mississippi’s law allowing timely-cast absentee ballots to be received and counted up to five business days after Election Day in federal general elections.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Election Day statutes (e.g., 2 U.S.C. §§ 7 and 1 (now recodified in Title 52)) and the U.S. Constitution’s Elections Clause and Presidential Electors Clause; challenged state law is Miss. Code Ann. § 23-15-637(1)(a) (the “Receipt Deadline”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Mississippi (through the Secretary of State) argues that the federal Election Day statutes do not forbid a state from accepting and counting ballots that were cast by Election Day but arrive shortly afterward, because those statutes set the day on which voting occurs, not the administrative deadline for receipt/counting of absentee ballots. Petitioner contends the Fifth Circuit misread this Court’s cases—especially Foster v. Love—by converting “Election Day” into a rigid federal receipt deadline, and that such a rule would destabilize longstanding election practices, invite confusion, and needlessly interfere with state authority under the Elections Clause and Electors Clause. Petitioner and supporting amici also stress congressional enactments like UOCAVA as consistent with (or affirmatively contemplating) post–Election Day ballot receipt in some contexts, and they invoke a purposive concern that Congress would not have intended Election Day statutes to impede voting.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (RNC and others who prevailed below) argue that Mississippi’s receipt deadline extends the election beyond the single, uniform federal Election Day required for congressional and presidential elections, because ballots arriving after Election Day can change outcomes and therefore mean the election is not finalized (i.e., “not consummated”) on the congressionally fixed day. They contend the Fifth Circuit correctly applied Foster’s core principle—that federal law requires the decisive act of choosing federal officers to be completed on Election Day—to hold that a state may not keep voting effectively open by counting ballots received afterward. Respondents also maintain that petitioner’s reliance on other Supreme Court decisions is misplaced because those cases did not address post–Election Day receipt in general elections, and that RNC v. DNC involved primaries where the federal Election Day statutes do not apply in the same way.
key_precedents: Republican National Committee v. Democratic National Committee (2020)
Voting Integrity Project, Inc. v. Bomer (5th Cir. 2000)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan’s central point—that §§1 and 7 do not expressly require receipt by Election Day and that Congress can write deadline rules when it wants—has force, but it does not supply the needed textual hook to treat ballots first received after the congressionally fixed “day” as votes legally cast on that day. The ordinary meaning of “the day … for the election” in the uniform-day statutes, reinforced by the settled understanding that Congress chose a single national day to prevent elections from being decided by returns coming in later, is that the State may not keep open the set of countable votes beyond that day. As Justice Thomas notes, receipt is not merely “ministerial”; it is a necessary condition for a ballot to have legal effect, and counting ballots that enter the system only after Election Day shifts the decisive act of choosing off the federal day in the way Foster condemns. The absence of an explicit federal receipt deadline cuts against overreading the statutes, but it cannot be converted into affirmative permission for States to extend, in operation, the time within which new, countable votes may arrive.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan press that §§1 and 7 do not expressly impose a receipt-by deadline, but that argument treats statutory silence as permission to extend the legally operative window for having votes counted beyond the congressionally fixed day. The uniform-day command Congress enacted is not merely about when a voter may mark a ballot; it is about when the election is held in a manner that determines the choice, and a ballot first received days later is not legally effective on Election Day in the relevant sense Chief Justice Roberts identifies. Justice Alito’s characterization of receipt as “ministerial” understates that receipt is a necessary condition to a vote’s legal effect and thus can keep the election open to post–Election Day inflows, the very mischief uniform-day legislation sought to prevent and that Foster’s “consummation” concept captures. Given that, I do not read the Election Day statutes to allow a State to treat the decisive set of countable votes as continuing to arrive after the federal day, absent a clearer congressional authorization.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Thomas press the best contrary point: that receipt is a necessary condition to a ballot’s legal effect, so accepting ballots received after Tuesday “extends” the election beyond the congressionally fixed day. But that argument still depends on converting §§1 and 7—statutes that set a uniform day for holding elections—into an implied federal receipt-by-midnight mandate that Congress did not express, despite knowing how to write explicit deadline rules when it wishes (as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize). Foster v. Love is not a close fit because it addressed a regime that consummated the choice before Election Day; treating short, definite post-day receipt of timely-cast ballots as forbidden would read Foster to uproot a long-pedigreed, facially neutral administrative practice without the clear congressional command we ordinarily require in this “time, place, and manner” domain. Mississippi’s fixed five-business-day window, tied to a postmark by Election Day, looks like part of the usual burdens and mechanics of absentee voting rather than a state effort to authorize voting after the federal day.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take seriously Chief Justice Roberts’s point (echoed by Justice Thomas) that receipt and counting are necessary for a vote’s legal effect, and that late-arriving ballots could be said to keep the election “open.” But the Election Day statutes fix the “day” the election is “held” and do not specify the consequence respondents urge—invalidating ballots timely cast by Election Day—so I am unwilling to infer a disenfranchising receipt-by-midnight rule from silence. As Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize, Congress has shown it can speak with precision when it wants to regulate ballot-handling deadlines, and Foster is best read to bar consummating the choice on a different day, not to prohibit a short, definite window for receiving ballots cast by the fixed day. Absent clearer statutory direction, courts should not impose their own coercive sanction by converting a day-setting statute into a rigid federal receipt deadline.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Thomas’s central claim is that because receipt is a precondition to counting, allowing post–Election Day receipt “extends” the election beyond the federally fixed day. But §§ 1 and 7 fix only the day the election is “held”; they do not add a further, judge-made receipt-by-midnight rule—especially when Congress has shown, in other election provisions, that it can specify precise ballot-handling deadlines when it wants to. Foster v. Love, as Justice Barrett notes, concerned a state scheme that consummated the choice before Election Day; treating ordinary post-day administration (including the counting of ballots timely cast by Election Day and arriving in a brief, definite window) as a forbidden “late election” stretches Foster and converts statutory silence into disenfranchisement. On this text and structure, the better reading is that Mississippi’s rule regulates how to count votes cast on the federal day, not when the federal election is held.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Thomas offer the most serious objection: that an “election” necessarily includes receipt and counting, so counting ballots first received after Tuesday makes the election effectively multi-day. But §§ 1 and 7 use the same operative term—“day”—to fix when the election is “held,” and nothing in that text supplies the additional receipt-by-midnight requirement respondents ask us to infer; under the presumption of consistent usage, it is difficult to treat “day” as sometimes meaning “voting” and sometimes “receipt and tabulation” without some textual cue. As Justice Barrett notes, Congress routinely writes explicit timing and receipt rules when it means to, and the absence of such language here—against the backdrop of longstanding post-day canvassing and processing—counsels against converting a day-setting statute into a freestanding federal receipt deadline. Foster, too, is best understood (as Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh explain) as preventing States from moving the decisive act of voting off the federal day, not from counting ballots timely cast by that day but received shortly thereafter pursuant to a fixed rule.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Thomas’s core point—that receipt is a necessary condition to legal effect, so accepting ballots after Tuesday necessarily “extends” the federal election—has force as a matter of practical operation. But the federal Election Day statutes set a uniform “day” on which the election is “held” and do not clearly impose the distinct, nationwide receipt-by-midnight rule respondents propose; converting that silence into a preemptive prohibition would displace a state legislature’s settled rule without the kind of clear congressional command we ordinarily require in this domain, as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize. Foster v. Love is best read to bar state systems that consummate the choice on a different day than Congress prescribed, not to invalidate counting of ballots timely cast by Election Day and received within a short, fixed period. On this record, Mississippi’s rule regulates post-Day administration of timely-cast votes rather than authorizing voting on a different day, so I would not extend Foster or infer preemption from statutory generality.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Thomas’s best point is that “holding” an election might be read to include receipt and counting, making a post–Election Day receipt window look like an extension of the election itself. But the federal Election Day statutes speak only in terms of a uniform “day” on which the election is “held,” and they do not clearly state the further, disenfranchising consequence respondents seek—a nationwide receipt-by-midnight rule that invalidates ballots timely cast by that day. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, when Congress intends to regulate ballot-handling mechanics and deadlines it does so expressly, and I find that structural comparison persuasive evidence that the silence here should not be converted into preemptive force. Foster v. Love is best read, as Justice Alito and others note, to prohibit consummating the choice on a different day than Congress set; counting ballots cast by Election Day but received shortly after is materially different from moving the decisive act of voting off that day.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Thomas’s best point is that an “election” could be understood as the legally operative collective choice, and that receipt is a necessary condition for legal effect—so counting ballots first received after Tuesday arguably keeps the election “open.” But reading §§ 1 and 7 naturally, in context, Congress fixed the day on which voting is to occur; it did not also enact (by silence) a nationwide receipt-by-midnight rule, especially given—as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan stress—that Congress elsewhere speaks expressly when it intends to regulate ballot-handling mechanics and deadlines. Mississippi’s rule functions as a mandatory precondition-to-relief (defining which ballots timely cast by Election Day qualify to be counted) rather than authorizing voting on a different day, and stretching Foster’s “consummation” concept to invalidate ordinary post–Election Day receipt and tabulation would convert a day-setting statute into a broad administrative code without textual footing. Absent a clearer congressional command, I remain unpersuaded that the federal scheme displaces this limited, definite receipt window for ballots cast by Election Day.

John Roberts.reasoning: The operative federal statutes fix the “day” for the “election” of Representatives and Senators and the “time” for appointing presidential electors, and the ordinary meaning of holding an election is not merely when a voter marks a ballot but when the vote is received and counted as part of the decisive act of choosing federal officers. Mississippi’s five-business-day post–Election Day receipt rule lacks a textual hook in those statutes and, as applied here, extends the legally operative act of casting a counted vote beyond the congressionally prescribed day, creating a direct conflict. That reading is confirmed by the Elections Clause’s structure—States regulate the “Times, Places and Manner” subject to Congress’s power to “make or alter” such regulations—and by the settled understanding, reflected in uniform-day legislation and practice, that Congress may require federal elections to be consummated on a single day. Nor do later statutes facilitating absentee voting supply a clear indication that Congress displaced the uniform-day command for general elections; any such change is for Congress to make expressly.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes fix a single day on which the decisive act of choosing federal officers must occur, and Mississippi’s rule requiring only that an absentee ballot be postmarked by Election Day but received and counted days later risks extending the effective period for casting votes beyond that day. Even if one can characterize the rule as a mere “receipt deadline,” in practice it keeps the election open after Congress’s chosen day and invites precisely the sort of uncertainty and post–Election Day alteration of outcomes that the Election Day statutes are meant to prevent. Consistent with my skepticism of judicially created late-election alterations, I would adhere to Congress’s status-quo command of a uniform Election Day rather than endorse state rules that permit ballots arriving after that day to decide federal elections. Foster v. Love supplies the governing principle that federal law precludes state regimes that move the operative federal election beyond the congressionally mandated day.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes fix a uniform day for holding federal elections, but they do not clearly speak to—much less unmistakably forbid—a State’s ministerial decision to count absentee ballots that were timely cast by Election Day and received within a short, definite period thereafter. Given the States’ constitutionally assigned authority over the “Times, Places and Manner” of federal elections, we should be reluctant to read these long-standing, facially neutral rules of election administration as preempted absent a far clearer congressional command—especially where many jurisdictions have historically accommodated mail-ballot transit time without treating that as “extending” voting. Mississippi’s five-business-day window is a modest, commonplace accommodation that mitigates the usual burdens of voting by mail, while still serving orderly administration through a fixed, limited deadline; construing federal law to invalidate it would needlessly destabilize widespread election practices. Foster v. Love does not compel the Fifth Circuit’s rigid receipt-by-election-day rule, because Foster addressed a system that effectively completed the choice of federal officers before Election Day, not the counting of ballots cast by Election Day but received shortly after.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I would begin with the text and structure of the federal “Election Day” statutes, which set “the day” for holding federal elections but do not specify a consequence that ballots timely cast by that day become invalid if received shortly afterward. Absent a clear statement that Congress made Election Day a rigid federal receipt deadline, I would not infer a coercive sanction—disenfranchisement of timely voters or a categorical loss of state administrative authority—especially where States traditionally administer mechanics like absentee-ballot handling under the Elections Clause. Mississippi’s rule does not authorize voting after Election Day; it accepts only ballots cast by Election Day and merely regulates post-day receipt and counting, so any conflict is at most a claimed-processing-type timing dispute that Congress did not clearly preempt. Foster v. Love requires that the decisive act of choosing occur on the congressionally set day, but it does not squarely compel treating modest post–Election Day receipt of timely-cast absentee ballots as extending the election itself in the absence of explicit statutory language to that effect.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Start with the operative text: the federal “Election Day” statutes fix a single day for holding federal elections, but they do not say that every ballot must be received or counted by that day, and I would not create a judge-made receipt-deadline carveout untethered to the statutory language. Read in real-world administrative context, Mississippi’s rule requires the voter’s decisive act—casting the ballot—to occur by Election Day and then allows a brief, uniform window for ordinary post-Election Day processing and mail delivery; that does not convert the election into a multi-day voting period. Foster v. Love addressed a different problem—states concluding ("consummating") the electoral choice before the federal day—so extending Foster to forbid counting timely-cast absentee ballots received shortly after Election Day stretches its principle past the text Congress enacted. And given Congress’s repeated election-administration interventions (including protections for mailed ballots in contexts like UOCAVA), the better reading is that Congress targeted nonuniform timing of the election itself, not routine receipt-and-counting mechanics that determine whether timely votes are “properly counted.”

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The operative federal texts require that congressional and presidential elections be held on “the Tuesday next after the 1st Monday” in November, and in ordinary usage that language fixes when votes must be cast, not the deadline by which election officials must finish the ministerial tasks of transporting, receiving, verifying, and counting ballots lawfully cast that day. Reading “election” to mean the entire administrative process through final tabulation would create atextual distinctions and practical anomalies across the same statutory scheme—where Congress spoke in terms of a uniform “day,” not a uniform “moment of final canvass”—and nothing in §§ 7 or 1 supplies a clear textual command converting Election Day into a federal receipt deadline. Against that text, longstanding state practice at the time Mississippi’s rule became commonplace (and Congress’s subsequent enactments in adjacent election statutes contemplating post–Election Day receipt in specified contexts) reinforces that Congress has not clearly displaced the background understanding that timely-cast ballots may be counted after Election Day. Foster’s concern was a State moving the decisive act of voting off the congressionally fixed day (there, concluding elections before Election Day), and it does not clearly resolve—much less foreclose—the narrower question whether ballots cast by Election Day may be received and counted shortly thereafter.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes require that the election be “held on” the congressionally specified Tuesday, which is best read—consistent with ordinary meaning and Foster v. Love—to regulate when voters must cast their ballots (the decisive act of choosing), not to impose a rigid federal deadline for the State’s administrative receipt and canvass of ballots timely cast by Election Day. Mississippi’s five-business-day receipt window for absentee ballots cast by Election Day does not move the election to a different day or authorize voting after Election Day; it sets a post-election counting rule, and Congress has not clearly displaced that kind of state election-administration choice for federal general elections. Treating any post–Election Day receipt of timely-cast ballots as per se unlawful would extend Foster beyond its predicate (a system that consummated the decisive choice before the federal day) and would improperly convert a uniform “day for the election” requirement into a federal receipt-by-midnight rule absent clear statutory text. Applying the structural Elections Clause framework, federal law controls where it speaks, but here it does not speak with the clarity necessary to preempt Mississippi’s legislature’s chosen method for counting ballots cast by Election Day.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes fix the “day” for holding federal elections, but they do not contain a clear statement tying that timing rule to the additional legal consequence respondents assert here—a federal receipt-by-Election-Day requirement for absentee ballots timely cast by Election Day. Reading the provisions in statutory context reinforces that point: when Congress intends to regulate ballot-handling mechanics (including deadlines), it knows how to do so expressly in adjacent election statutes, and the absence of comparable language here counsels against implying a preemptive receipt deadline. Foster v. Love supplies, at most, the rule that a State may not consummate (i.e., definitively determine) an election before the federally fixed day; it does not clearly speak to post–Election Day administrative receipt/counting of ballots cast on time. And under the Supremacy Clause conflict-preemption baseline, respondents have not offered a sufficiently concrete, textually grounded interpretation showing that counting timely-cast ballots received within five business days makes it impossible to comply with the federal mandate to hold the election on Election Day.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Reading the federal “Election Day” statutes naturally, in context, and as part of the broader election-administration scheme Congress has enacted, they fix a uniform day for the act of choosing federal officers, not an across-the-board federal deadline for the receipt and counting of timely-cast absentee ballots. Respondents’ contrary rule depends on a risky negative inference from statutory silence—treating the absence of an express “receipt-by” command as an implicit prohibition—despite contextual indicators that Congress has repeatedly legislated to protect absentee voting and accommodate practical administration (including post–Election Day processing) in related statutes. Functionally, Mississippi’s five-business-day receipt window operates as an administrative, mandatory precondition to counting (a scope rule for what ballots qualify), not as an extension of “voting” beyond Election Day, because the voter’s decisive act occurs when the ballot is timely cast by Election Day. Foster’s “consummation” principle targets state schemes that make the final selection occur on a different day (e.g., effectively electing before or after the federally fixed day), and it does not compel converting Election Day into a rigid federal receipt deadline absent clear congressional instruction.
